items.prompt: Find the volume of the solid generated when the region R is revolved about the x-axis.
steps: Washers: the outer radius is 4e^(−x/2) and the inner radius is x^2/2.
items.skill: Compute a washer volume about the x-axis

items.prompt: Find the volume of the solid generated when the region R is revolved about the horizontal line y = 5.
steps: The line y = 5 lies above R, so the far boundary is y = x^2/2, with R = 5 − x^2/2, and the near boundary is y = 4e^(−x/2), with r = 5 − 4e^(−x/2).
items.skill: Compute a washer volume about a line above the region

items.prompt: A solid stands on the region R, and every slice of it cut perpendicular to the x-axis is a square whose side runs across R. Find the volume of the solid.
steps: A square's side is the vertical extent of R: s(x) = 4e^(−x/2) − x^2/2.
Volume = ∫ from 0 to q of (4e^(−x/2) − x^2/2)^2 dx ≈ 10.277.
items.skill: Compute a volume with square cross sections

items.prompt: Let k = q^2/2 be the y-coordinate of the intersection point. Which expression gives the area of R using horizontal slices?
choices: ∫ from 0 to k of √(2y) dy + ∫ from k to 4 of (−2ln(y/4)) dy
∫ from 0 to k of (−2ln(y/4)) dy + ∫ from k to 4 of √(2y) dy
items.answer: (B) ∫ from 0 to k of √(2y) dy + ∫ from k to 4 of (−2ln(y/4)) dy
steps: Solve each boundary for x: y = x^2/2 gives x = √(2y), and y = 4e^(−x/2) gives x = −2ln(y/4).
Below y = k the right boundary of R is x = √(2y); above y = k it is x = −2ln(y/4); the left boundary is x = 0 throughout. That gives the sum of two integrals, which also evaluates to about 3.775.
items.skill: Set up an area with horizontal slices

items.prompt: The graphs of y = sin x and y = x^3 − 2x enclose two regions. (a) Find the x-coordinates of all intersection points of the two graphs. (b) Write an expression involving one or more integrals for the total area of the two regions. (c) Find the total area.

rubric.criterion: (b) Uses the correct top function on each interval: x^3 − 2x on [−1.618, 0] and sin x on [0, 1.618] (or ∫ |sin x − (x^3 − 2x)| dx).
(b) Uses the intersection values as limits.
(c) Total area ≈ 3.903.

items.answer: (a) x ≈ −1.618, 0, and 1.618. (b) ∫ from −1.618 to 0 of (x^3 − 2x − sin x) dx + ∫ from 0 to 1.618 of (sin x − x^3 + 2x) dx. (c) About 3.903.
steps: Solve sin x = x^3 − 2x: x = 0 and x ≈ ±1.618 (store the positive root as Q).
Test a point: at x = 1, sin 1 ≈ 0.841 > 1 − 2 = −1, so sin x is on top on (0, Q); by symmetry (both functions are odd) x^3 − 2x is on top on (−Q, 0).
Total area = ∫ from −Q to Q of |sin x − (x^3 − 2x)| dx ≈ 3.903; the signed integral is 0, so the absolute value matters.
items.skill: Find an area with more than two intersections

weeks.title: Practice exam, self-scoring, and error analysis
weeks.objective: Take the full-length practice exam in two timed sittings, score it with the key and the scoring guidelines, record raw points by section and unit, and classify and correct every lost point.

connection.before: Weeks 30–32 reviewed Units 1–8 by theme and practiced the exam's no-calculator and calculator pacing.
connection.after: Week 34 uses this week's raw-point tally and error log to choose targeted review.

days: Section I of the practice exam in one sitting: Part A, 29 multiple-choice questions in 62 minutes with no calculator, then Part B, 13 questions in 38 minutes with a graphing calculator.
Section II of the practice exam in one sitting: Part A, 2 free-response questions in 30 minutes with a graphing calculator, then Part B, 4 questions in 60 minutes with no calculator.
Score Section I with the key, record raw points by part and by unit, and read the rationale for every missed or guessed question.
Practice applying scoring guidelines (Worksheet A), then score your own Section II question by question and part by part.
Error analysis (Worksheets B and C): classify each lost point by cause, rework those items from a blank page, and draft next week's plan.
explanation: This week is the full-length practice exam in the May 2027 format. Section I has 42 multiple-choice questions: Part A, 29 questions in 62 minutes with no calculator, and Part B, 13 questions in 38 minutes with a graphing calculator required. Section II has 6 free-response questions worth 9 points each: Part A, 2 questions in 30 minutes with a graphing calculator, and Part B, 4 questions in 60 minutes without one. Take it under real timing, with no notes and no formula sheet, because the exam supplies none, and use the calculator only in the parts that allow it. Do not open the key until both sections are finished. On the real exam, multiple choice is answered in the Bluebook app and free response is handwritten; this practice exam is printed, so mark the answer sheet as you go.

Score honestly, in raw points. Multiple choice earns 1 point per correct answer with no penalty for a wrong one, so no question should be left blank. Free-response parts are scored with the scoring guidelines: a point is earned only when the response shows what the criterion describes, so a correct number reached by an unsupported method, or a decimal with no setup, may earn nothing. Record raw points by section, by question, and by unit in the key's tally table. These are raw practice points only: they are not an AP® score and are not converted to one.

Error analysis turns a tally into a plan. For each lost point, write the item number, its unit, and one cause: concept (the idea was missing or wrong), procedure (an algebra, derivative, or integral slip), reading (the question asked for something else, or a graph or table was misread), justification (right idea, incomplete reason), calculator (mode, setup, or a value rounded too early), or time (not reached). Then rework the item from a blank page without the key. Patterns matter more than single misses: three lost justification points across different questions call for writing practice, not more content review.

When you check free response, compare your work with each rubric row, not only with the final answer. Points are commonly lost for missing units on a contextual answer, a reason about the wrong function, a missing initial amount in an accumulation, a constant of integration added after solving for y, a relative extremum given when an absolute one was asked for, and decimals rounded before the last step. Calculator answers need three decimal places, and the integral or equation must appear before the number.

examples.prompt: A free-response part worth 3 points reads: "The volume of water in a tank changes at the rate V′(t) = 8 − 2t liters per minute for 0 ≤ t ≤ 6, and V(0) = 20 liters. Find the maximum volume of water in the tank on 0 ≤ t ≤ 6. Justify your answer." Its rubric: 1 point for V′(t) = 0 at t = 4; 1 point for a justification (V′ changes from positive to negative at t = 4, or a candidates test); 1 point for the maximum volume, 36 liters. A student writes: "V′(t) = 8 − 2t = 0 at t = 4. V′ is positive then negative there, so it is a maximum. V(4) = 8(4) − 4^2 = 16 liters." Score the response.
examples.answer: 2 of 3 points: the first two points are earned, but the maximum volume is wrong because the response leaves out the initial 20 liters; the maximum is V(4) = 20 + 16 = 36 liters.
steps: Point 1: the response solves V′(t) = 0 and gets t = 4. Earned.
Point 2: "V′ is positive then negative" names the right function and its sign change. Earned.
Point 3: V(4) = V(0) + ∫ from 0 to 4 of (8 − 2t) dt = 20 + 16 = 36 liters; the response reports 16, the change in volume rather than the volume. Not earned.

examples.prompt: Graphing calculator. A student needs ∫ from 0 to 1.5 of sin(x^2) dx and reports 0.020. Explain the likely error, and find the correct value.
examples.answer: The calculator was in degree mode, which treats x^2 as degrees; in radian mode the integral is about 0.778.
steps: In degree mode, sin(x^2) means sin of x^2 degrees, about sin((π/180)x^2) ≈ (π/180)x^2 for small angles, so the integral is close to (π/180)(1.5^3/3) ≈ 0.0196, which matches 0.020.
Calculus answers use radians. Switch the calculator to radian mode and recompute.
∫ from 0 to 1.5 of sin(x^2) dx ≈ 0.778 in radian mode.

worksheets.title: Scoring free response with a rubric
worksheets.directions: No calculator. Each item gives a free-response part, its rubric, and a student response. Decide how many points the response earns, and explain each point earned or lost with the rubric's wording.

items.prompt: A 2-point part reads: "The function f has derivative f′(x) = (x − 2)(x + 1)^2. Find the x-coordinate of each relative extremum of f, classify it, and justify your answer." Rubric: 1 point for a relative minimum at x = 2 and no other relative extremum; 1 point for the justification that f′ changes from negative to positive at x = 2. A student writes: "f′ = 0 at x = 2 and x = −1. f′ changes from negative to positive at x = 2, so f has a relative minimum there, and f has a relative maximum at x = −1." How many points does the response earn?
items.answer: 1 of 2 points: the justification point is earned, but the first point is lost because the response also claims a relative maximum at x = −1.
steps: f′(x) = (x − 2)(x + 1)^2 is negative on both sides of x = −1, so f has no extremum there; claiming one violates the first rubric row.
The sentence about x = 2 names f′ and its sign change correctly, so the justification point is earned.
items.skill: Score a justification of extrema

items.prompt: A 2-point part reads: "R(t) is the rate, in liters per minute, at which water drains from a tank, where t is in minutes. What does ∫ from 0 to 30 of R(t) dt = 450 tell you about the tank?" Rubric: 1 point for identifying the amount of water that drains out of the tank; 1 point for the time interval 0 ≤ t ≤ 30 minutes together with the units, liters. A student writes: "There are 450 liters of water left in the tank at t = 30 minutes." How many points does the response earn?
items.answer: 0 of 2 points: the response describes the amount remaining at one instant, not the amount that drained out during the first 30 minutes.
steps: The integral of a draining rate is the amount that leaves, so "left in the tank" misidentifies the quantity: the first point is not earned.
"At t = 30" names an instant rather than the interval 0 ≤ t ≤ 30, so the second point is not earned even though liters is mentioned.
items.skill: Score a contextual interpretation of an integral

items.prompt: A 2-point calculator part reads: "Find the area of the region enclosed by the graphs of y = 4 − x^2 and y = e^x." Rubric: 1 point for an integral with correct limits (x ≈ −1.965 and x ≈ 1.058) and integrand 4 − x^2 − e^x; 1 point for the answer 6.428 (accept 6.427–6.429). A student writes only: "Area = 6.43." How many points does the response earn, and how should it be rewritten?
items.answer: 0 of 2 points: there is no integral, and 6.43 is not given to three decimal places. A full response is: Area = ∫ from −1.965 to 1.058 of (4 − x^2 − e^x) dx ≈ 6.428.
steps: The first point needs a written integral; a calculator result alone shows no setup.
The second point needs a value correct to three decimal places; 6.43 is outside 6.427–6.429 as written, so it does not earn the point.
items.skill: Score a calculator response without a setup

items.prompt: A 4-point part reads: "Find the particular solution y = f(x) of dy/dx = 2xy with f(0) = 3." Rubric: 1 point for separating variables; 1 point for antiderivatives; 1 point for the constant of integration and using the initial condition; 1 point for solving for y. A response with no constant of integration before solving for y earns at most 2 points. A student writes: "dy/y = 2x dx, so ln y = x^2. Then y = e^(x^2) + C, and 3 = 1 + C, so C = 2 and y = e^(x^2) + 2." How many points does the response earn, and what is the correct solution?
items.answer: 2 of 4 points (separation and antiderivatives). The constant was added after exponentiating, so the last two points are lost. The correct solution is y = 3e^(x^2).
steps: Separation dy/y = 2x dx and the antiderivatives ln y and x^2 are correct: 2 points.
ln|y| = x^2 + C gives y = Ae^(x^2); with f(0) = 3, A = 3. Adding C after exponentiating produces a function that does not solve the equation, so the rubric caps the score at 2.
items.skill: Score a separable-equation response

items.prompt: A 2-point part reads: "H is differentiable, H(2) = 5, and H(8) = 14. Must there be a value c in (2, 8) with H′(c) = 1.5? Justify." Rubric: 1 point for (H(8) − H(2))/(8 − 2) = 1.5; 1 point for stating that H is differentiable (so continuous) and applying the Mean Value Theorem. A student writes: "Yes, by the Mean Value Theorem, because (14 − 5)/(8 − 2) = 1.5." How many points does the response earn?
items.answer: 1 of 2 points: the difference quotient is correct, but the response never states the hypothesis that H is differentiable and therefore continuous.
steps: (14 − 5)/6 = 1.5 earns the first point.
Naming the theorem is not enough; the second point requires the conditions that make it apply.
items.skill: Score a Mean Value Theorem justification

items.prompt: A 2-point part reads: "A particle has velocity v(t) = t^2 − 7. Find its acceleration at t = 2. Is the speed of the particle increasing or decreasing at t = 2? Give a reason." Rubric: 1 point for a(2) = 4; 1 point for "decreasing, because v(2) and a(2) have opposite signs." A student writes: "a(t) = 2t, so a(2) = 4 > 0, so the speed is increasing." How many points does the response earn?
items.answer: 1 of 2 points: a(2) = 4 is correct, but the speed is decreasing because v(2) = −3 < 0 while a(2) > 0.
steps: The first point is earned for a(2) = 4.
Positive acceleration alone does not mean speeding up; with v(2) = −3 the signs differ, so the speed decreases. The second point is not earned.
items.skill: Score a speed argument

worksheets.title: Error analysis: no-calculator work
worksheets.directions: No calculator. Each item shows work with an error. Name the error, then give a corrected solution.

items.prompt: A student writes: d/dx [cos^3(2x)] = −3cos^2(2x)·sin(2x). Find and correct the error.
items.answer: The derivative of the innermost function 2x is missing. Correct: d/dx [cos^3(2x)] = 3cos^2(2x)·(−sin(2x))·2 = −6cos^2(2x)·sin(2x).
steps: The function has three layers: a cube, a cosine, and 2x; the chain rule needs a factor from each.
The factor 2 from d/dx(2x) was dropped.
items.skill: Find a missing chain-rule factor

items.prompt: A student evaluates lim as x→0 of cos x/(x + 1) with L'Hospital's Rule and writes lim as x→0 of (−sin x)/1 = 0. Find and correct the error.
items.answer: The limit is not an indeterminate form, so L'Hospital's Rule does not apply. Substitution gives cos 0/(0 + 1) = 1.
steps: At x = 0 the numerator is 1 and the denominator is 1, so the form is 1/1, not 0/0 or ∞/∞.
For a continuous quotient with a nonzero denominator, the limit is the value: 1.
items.skill: Check the form before using L'Hospital's Rule

items.prompt: A student evaluates ∫ from 0 to 1 of x(x^2 + 1)^3 dx with u = x^2 + 1 and writes (1/2)∫ from 0 to 1 of u^3 du = 1/8. Find and correct the error.
items.answer: The limits were not changed to u-values. With u from 1 to 2: (1/2)∫ from 1 to 2 of u^3 du = (1/8)(16 − 1) = 15/8.
steps: When x = 0, u = 1; when x = 1, u = 2.
items.skill: Change the limits in a substitution

items.prompt: The function f is invertible, with f(1) = 4, f′(1) = 5, and f′(4) = 2. Let g be the inverse of f. A student writes g′(4) = 1/f′(4) = 1/2. Which statement identifies the error?
choices: The derivative of f must be evaluated at g(4) = 1, so g′(4) = 1/5.
The reciprocal should not be taken, so g′(4) = 2.
items.answer: (A) The derivative of f must be evaluated at g(4) = 1, so g′(4) = 1/5.
steps: g′(b) = 1/f′(g(b)); here g(4) = 1 because f(1) = 4.
items.skill: Diagnose an inverse-derivative error

items.prompt: A particle has velocity v(t) = t − 2 for 0 ≤ t ≤ 4. A student finds the total distance traveled as ∫ from 0 to 4 of (t − 2) dt = 0. Find and correct the error.
items.answer: The integral of v gives displacement, not distance. Distance = ∫ from 0 to 4 of |t − 2| dt = 2 + 2 = 4.
steps: v < 0 on (0, 2) and v > 0 on (2, 4), so the motion reverses at t = 2 and the signed areas cancel.
Each triangle has area 2, so the distance is 4.
items.skill: Separate distance from displacement

items.prompt: Sand forms a conical pile whose height is always twice its radius. Sand is added at 6 cubic centimeters per second. A student finds how fast the radius grows when r = 3 cm by writing V = (π/3)(3)^2h = 3πh, so dV/dt = 3π(dh/dt), giving dh/dt = 2/π and dr/dt = 1/π cm/s. (a) Identify the error. (b) Find the correct rate.

rubric.criterion: (a) Names the error: r was replaced by 3 before differentiating, treating the radius as constant while it changes.
(b) Writes V in one variable, V = (π/3)r^2(2r) = (2π/3)r^3, and differentiates: dV/dt = 2πr^2(dr/dt).

items.answer: (a) Substituting r = 3 before differentiating freezes a changing quantity. (b) dr/dt = 1/(3π) cm/s, about 0.106 cm/s.
steps: The equation must hold at every instant before any instant's values are substituted.
With h = 2r, V = (2π/3)r^3 and dV/dt = 2πr^2(dr/dt).
6 = 2π(9)(dr/dt), so dr/dt = 1/(3π).
items.skill: Repair a related-rates solution

worksheets.title: Error analysis: calculator work
worksheets.directions: Graphing calculator. Each item shows calculator work with an error. Explain the error, then give the correct result to three decimal places with its setup.

items.prompt: A student uses the calculator's numerical derivative to find f′(1) for f(x) = x·tan x and reports 0.035. Explain the error and find f′(1).
items.answer: The calculator was in degree mode. In radians, f′(1) = tan 1 + sec^2 1 ≈ 4.983.
steps: In degree mode tan x is tan of x degrees, which is nearly linear with slope π/180 near 1, giving about 0.035.
In radian mode the numerical derivative of x·tan x at x = 1 is about 4.983 (exactly tan 1 + sec^2 1).
items.skill: Detect a degree-mode derivative

items.prompt: A student finds that y = e^x and y = 3 − x^2 intersect at x ≈ −1.677 and x ≈ 0.834, rounds these to −1.7 and 0.8, and then computes ∫ from −1.7 to 0.8 of (3 − x^2 − e^x) dx = 3.649. Explain the error and find the area of the region enclosed by the graphs.
items.answer: Rounding the limits before integrating changes the third decimal place. With the stored intersection values, the area is about 3.652.
steps: Store the intersections (for example as A and B) instead of retyping rounded values.
∫ from A to B of (3 − x^2 − e^x) dx ≈ 3.652, which differs from 3.649 in the third decimal place.
items.skill: Avoid premature rounding

items.prompt: A tank holds 120 liters of water at t = 0, and water flows in at r(t) = 5 + 3sin t liters per minute. A student reports the amount in the tank at t = 6 as ∫ from 0 to 6 of r(t) dt = 30.119 liters. Explain the error and find the correct amount.
items.answer: The initial 120 liters is missing. Amount = 120 + ∫ from 0 to 6 of r(t) dt ≈ 150.119 liters.
steps: The integral of the rate is the change in the amount, not the amount.
Add the starting value: 120 + 30.119 = 150.119 liters.
items.skill: Include the initial amount

items.prompt: Let A(t) = ∫ from 0 to t of ln(2 + s^2) ds. Asked for the rate of change of A at t = 2, a student reports ∫ from 0 to 2 of ln(2 + s^2) ds ≈ 2.286. Explain the error and find the rate.
items.answer: That value is A(2), not A′(2). By the Fundamental Theorem, A′(2) = ln(2 + 4) = ln 6 ≈ 1.792.
steps: The rate of change of an accumulation function is its integrand evaluated at the upper limit.
items.skill: Separate an accumulation from its rate

items.prompt: The region R is bounded by y = 2√x and y = x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 4. A student finds the volume of the solid generated when R is revolved about the line y = −2 by computing π∫ from 0 to 4 of ((2√x + 2) − (x + 2))^2 dx ≈ 6.702. Explain the error and find the volume.
items.answer: Washers need the difference of the squares of the radii, not the square of their difference. Volume = π∫ from 0 to 4 of [(2√x + 2)^2 − (x + 2)^2] dx ≈ 67.021.
steps: The outer radius is 2√x + 2 and the inner radius is x + 2 (distances from y = −2).
π∫ (R^2 − r^2) dx ≈ 67.021; π∫ (R − r)^2 dx gives a different, wrong value.
items.skill: Correct a washer-volume setup

items.prompt: A particle moves along a line with velocity v(t) = 2sin t − t/2 for 0 < t < 6. A student says the particle changes direction at t ≈ 1.318 and t ≈ 4.965, the solutions of a(t) = 2cos t − 1/2 = 0. Explain the error and find when the particle changes direction.
items.answer: The particle changes direction where v changes sign, not where a = 0. On (0, 6), v changes sign only at t ≈ 2.475.
steps: Zeros of a are where the velocity has extreme values.
Solving 2sin t − t/2 = 0 on (0, 6) gives t ≈ 2.475, where v changes from positive to negative.
items.skill: Locate direction changes from velocity

weeks.title: Targeted review from practice-exam results
weeks.objective: Use the practice exam's raw-point tally and error log to choose targeted practice in justification writing, table and graph reasoning, and calculator setups, and rework every missed item.

connection.before: Week 33's practice exam, its raw-point tally by section and unit, and the error log of causes.
connection.after: The exam itself follows; week 35 then begins a modeling investigation beyond the exam.

days: Rank units by raw points lost and causes by frequency; choose the two worksheets below that match the largest causes.
Worksheet A: justification language for theorems, extrema, concavity, and differential equations.
Worksheet B: reasoning from graphs and tables of rates, accumulations, and estimates.
Worksheet C: calculator setups; then rework every missed practice-exam item from a blank page.
Light review only: check exam logistics (radian mode, a charged calculator, the timing plan) and rest.
explanation: A raw-point tally by unit shows where points went, and the error log shows why. Combine them: a unit with many points lost to procedure slips needs drill; points lost to justification need writing practice; points lost at the end of a part point to pacing. Choose the two largest causes and spend this week on them instead of rereading everything. Rework each missed practice-exam item from a blank page without the key and check it only afterward; an item you can now finish unaided has been fixed.

Justification language has a pattern: conclusion, reason, and the function the reason is about. "f has a relative maximum at x = c because f′ changes from positive to negative at x = c." "The graph of f is concave up on (a, b) because f′ is increasing there." "Because f is differentiable on (a, b) and continuous on [a, b], the Mean Value Theorem gives c in (a, b) with f′(c) = (f(b) − f(a))/(b − a)." "Because r is continuous on [a, b] and r(a) < k < r(b), the Intermediate Value Theorem gives c in (a, b) with r(c) = k." "The tangent-line approximation is an underestimate because the graph is concave up." Each sentence names a hypothesis or a sign, and each fails without it.

Representations carry most of the points on graph and table questions. From a table, estimate a derivative with the closest values that bracket the input and attach units; use the table's own widths in Riemann and trapezoidal sums; apply the Intermediate Value Theorem or the Mean Value Theorem only when continuity or differentiability is given. From a graph of a rate, net change is signed area (computed with geometry), the amount is greatest where the rate changes from positive to negative, and the average value differs from the average rate of change.

Calculator parts reward setups. Before each number, write the equation solved, the derivative evaluated, or the integral computed, and store intermediate values. The four calculator skills the exam relies on are graphing in a suitable window, solving an equation or finding an intersection, evaluating a numerical derivative at a point, and evaluating a numerical integral. Check radian mode at the start of every calculator part.

figures.alt: Graph of y = r(t) for 0 ≤ t ≤ 8, made of line segments joining the points (0, 2), (2, 4), (4, 0), (6, −2), and (8, 0).
figures.caption: Rate r(t), in liters per minute

examples.prompt: A student's practice-exam tally shows these lost points: Unit 5, 5 of 8 multiple-choice points and 4 justification points in free response; Unit 6, 2 multiple-choice points; Unit 8, 3 points on calculator parts (two from rounding intersection values, one from degree mode). Which two worksheets should the student do first, and why?
examples.answer: Worksheet A (justification language) and Worksheet C (calculator setups): those match the two largest causes, justification and calculator habits.
steps: Group lost points by cause: justification (4) and Unit 5 multiple choice (5) point to analysis reasoning; calculator habits (3) are a separate cause.
Worksheet A practices complete justifications, which also helps Unit 5 multiple choice.
Worksheet C practices storing values and mode checks, which address all three calculator points; the two Unit 6 points can be reworked directly.

examples.prompt: Let g(x) = ∫ from 0 to x of f(t) dt, where f is continuous and f(t) < 0 for 1 < t < 4. A student writes: "Since the derivative is negative, it is decreasing." Rewrite the sentence as a complete justification.
examples.answer: "g is decreasing on (1, 4) because g′(x) = f(x) < 0 for 1 < x < 4."
steps: Name the function that is decreasing: g, not "it".
Name the derivative and why it is negative: g′(x) = f(x) by the Fundamental Theorem, and f < 0 on (1, 4).
State the interval the conclusion holds on.

examples.prompt: Graphing calculator. The temperature of a greenhouse is P(t) = 3 + 2cos(t^2/8) degrees above the outside temperature, t hours after noon. Write a complete calculator response for the average of P over 0 ≤ t ≤ 4.
examples.answer: Average = (1/4)∫ from 0 to 4 of (3 + 2cos(t^2/8)) dt ≈ 4.335 degrees.
steps: State the definition: the average value of P on [0, 4] is (1/(4 − 0))∫ from 0 to 4 of P(t) dt.
Evaluate the integral in radian mode: about 17.341.
Divide by 4 and round only at the end: about 4.335 degrees.

worksheets.title: Justification language
worksheets.directions: No calculator. Write each conclusion as a complete sentence that names the function, its sign or change, and any theorem's hypotheses.

items.prompt: Functions f and g are continuous on [1, 5], with f(1) = 4, g(1) = 6, f(5) = 9, and g(5) = 7. Show that the graphs of f and g intersect at some x in (1, 5).
items.answer: Let h(x) = f(x) − g(x), which is continuous on [1, 5]. h(1) = −2 < 0 < 2 = h(5), so by the Intermediate Value Theorem h(c) = 0 for some c in (1, 5); there f(c) = g(c).
steps: A difference of continuous functions is continuous.
h(1) = 4 − 6 = −2 and h(5) = 9 − 7 = 2 have opposite signs, so the theorem gives a zero of h.
items.skill: Justify an intersection with the IVT

items.prompt: A train's position s(t), in kilometers, is a differentiable function of time t, in hours. s(0) = 0 and s(0.5) = 42. Show that at some moment the train's velocity is exactly 84 kilometers per hour.
items.answer: s is differentiable, hence continuous, on [0, 0.5]. By the Mean Value Theorem there is c in (0, 0.5) with s′(c) = (42 − 0)/(0.5 − 0) = 84 km/h.
steps: State the hypotheses: differentiable on (0, 0.5) and continuous on [0, 0.5].
The average velocity is 42/0.5 = 84 km/h, so the instantaneous velocity equals 84 km/h at some c.
items.skill: Apply the Mean Value Theorem in context

items.prompt: A function f has f(3) = 2, f′(3) = −1, and f″(x) = −x^2 for all x. Use the tangent line at x = 3 to approximate f(3.2), and decide whether the approximation is an overestimate or an underestimate. Justify.
items.answer: f(3.2) ≈ 2 − 0.2 = 1.8, an overestimate, because f″(x) = −x^2 < 0 near x = 3 makes the graph concave down, so the tangent line lies above it.
steps: f″ < 0 for x ≠ 0, so the graph is concave down on an interval containing 3 and 3.2.
items.skill: Justify a tangent-line estimate with concavity

items.prompt: The derivative of g is g′(x) = (x − 2)e^x for all x. Find the absolute minimum of g on (−∞, ∞) in terms of its location, and justify that it is absolute, not only relative.
items.answer: g has its absolute minimum at x = 2: g′ < 0 for all x < 2 and g′ > 0 for all x > 2, so g decreases up to x = 2 and increases afterward.
steps: e^x > 0, so g′ has the sign of x − 2; x = 2 is the only critical point.
Because g decreases on all of (−∞, 2) and increases on all of (2, ∞), g(2) is below every other value, not only nearby ones.
items.skill: Justify an absolute extremum with one critical point

items.prompt: The derivative f′ is increasing on (1, 3) and decreasing on (3, 5). Which sentence is a complete justification that the graph of f has a point of inflection at x = 3?
choices: The graph of f has a point of inflection at x = 3 because f′(3) = 0.
The graph of f has a point of inflection at x = 3 because f′ changes from increasing to decreasing there.
The graph of f has a point of inflection at x = 3 because f changes from increasing to decreasing there.
The graph of f has a point of inflection at x = 3 because f″(3) exists.
items.answer: (B) The graph of f has a point of inflection at x = 3 because f′ changes from increasing to decreasing there.
steps: Concavity of f changes exactly where f′ changes between increasing and decreasing.
f′(3) = 0 or a change in f's direction describes extrema, not inflection points.
items.skill: Recognize a complete inflection-point justification

items.prompt: Let y = f(x) be the solution of dy/dx = (y − 2)(x + 1) through the point (0, 1). Find d^2y/dx^2 at (0, 1), and decide whether the tangent-line approximation of f(0.1) is an overestimate or an underestimate.
items.answer: d^2y/dx^2 = −2 at (0, 1), so the solution is concave down there and the tangent-line approximation overestimates f(0.1).
steps: d^2y/dx^2 = (dy/dx)(x + 1) + (y − 2) by the product rule.
items.skill: Use a second derivative from a differential equation

worksheets.title: Representations: graphs and tables
worksheets.directions: No calculator. Items 1, 2, 3, and 6 use the graph of r shown: r(t) is the rate, in liters per minute, at which the volume of water in a tank changes, and the tank holds 10 liters at t = 0. Use geometry for areas.

items.prompt: Using the graph of r, how much water is in the tank at t = 8 minutes?
steps: Volume at t = 8 is 10 + ∫ from 0 to 8 of r(t) dt.
Areas: 6 on [0, 2] (a trapezoid), 4 on [2, 4], −2 on [4, 6], and −2 on [6, 8]; the sum is 6.
10 + 6 = 16 liters.
items.skill: Find an amount from a graph of its rate

items.prompt: Using the graph of r, at what time in [0, 8] is the volume of water greatest? Find that volume and justify your answer.
steps: The volume increases while r > 0 (0 < t < 4) and decreases while r < 0 (4 < t < 8), so r changing from positive to negative at t = 4 gives the maximum on [0, 8].
Volume at t = 4: 10 + 6 + 4 = 20 liters, which exceeds the endpoint values 10 and 16.
items.skill: Locate a maximum amount from a rate graph

items.prompt: Using the graph of r, find r′(5). What does r′(5) tell you about the rate at which the volume changes? Include units.
items.answer: r′(5) = −1 liter per minute per minute: at t = 5 the rate at which the volume changes is decreasing by 1 liter per minute each minute.
steps: On [4, 6] the graph is a segment from (4, 0) to (6, −2), with slope −2/2 = −1.
r is in liters per minute and t in minutes, so r′ is in liters per minute per minute.
items.skill: Interpret the slope of a rate graph

items.prompt:
A differentiable function f has the values shown.

| x | 0 | 1 | 3 | 4 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| f(x) | 2 | 5 | 5 | −1 |

Which statement must be true?
choices: f′(c) = 3 for exactly one c in (0, 1).
steps: f(1) = f(3) = 5 and f is differentiable, so the Mean Value Theorem on [1, 3] gives f′(c) = 0/2 = 0 for some c in (1, 3).
6 is not between any two listed values, the theorem gives at least one c (not exactly one), and the table cannot show that f is increasing.
items.skill: Draw conclusions from a table with theorems

items.prompt:
A cyclist's velocity v(t), in meters per second, is positive and is recorded at selected times.

| t (s) | 0 | 10 | 25 | 30 | 50 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| v(t) (m/s) | 4 | 6 | 7 | 5 | 3 |

(a) Estimate the cyclist's acceleration at t = 27, with units. (b) Use a left Riemann sum with the four subintervals to estimate ∫ from 0 to 50 of v(t) dt, and explain its meaning.
items.answer: (a) About −0.4 m/s^2. (b) About 265 meters: the approximate distance the cyclist travels during the 50 seconds.
steps: Because v > 0, the integral of velocity is the distance traveled, in meters.
items.skill: Estimate from a table of velocities

items.prompt: Using the graph of r, find the average rate of change of r on [2, 6] and the average value of r on [2, 6]. Explain in a sentence why they differ.
items.answer: Average rate of change: −3/2 liters per minute per minute. Average value: 1/2 liter per minute. The first describes how fast the rate itself changes; the second is the constant rate that would produce the same net change in volume.
steps: Average rate of change = (r(6) − r(2))/(6 − 2) = (−2 − 4)/4 = −3/2.
Average value = (1/4)∫ from 2 to 6 of r(t) dt = (1/4)(4 − 2) = 1/2.
items.skill: Distinguish average value from average rate of change

worksheets.title: Calculator setups
worksheets.directions: Graphing calculator in radian mode. Write the equation, derivative, or integral first, then the value to three decimal places, with units in context.

items.prompt: A phone's battery charge is B(t) = 100 − 85e^(−0.04t) percent, t minutes after it is plugged in. At what time is the battery charging at 2 percent per minute?
steps: Write the equation first: B′(t) = 2, with B′(t) = 85(0.04)e^(−0.04t) = 3.4e^(−0.04t).
Solve 3.4e^(−0.04t) = 2 (by calculator, or t = ln(1.7)/0.04): t ≈ 13.266 minutes.
items.skill: Solve for the time a rate reaches a value

items.prompt: The height of the tide at a harbor is H(t) = 1.8 + 1.2sin(πt/6.2) meters, t hours after midnight. Find H′(4), and interpret it with units.
items.answer: H′(4) ≈ −0.268 meters per hour: at 4 a.m. the tide is falling at about 0.268 meters per hour.
steps: Use the numerical derivative of H at t = 4 (radian mode): H′(4) ≈ −0.268.
Units are meters per hour, and the negative sign means the water level is going down.
items.skill: Evaluate and interpret a derivative in context

items.prompt: Wind speed at a ridge is modeled by w(t) = 12 + 4sin(t/2) + 0.3t kilometers per hour for 0 ≤ t ≤ 10 hours. Find the average wind speed over this period.
items.answer: (1/10)∫ from 0 to 10 of w(t) dt ≈ 14.073 km/h
steps: Average value = (1/(10 − 0))∫ from 0 to 10 of w(t) dt.
The integral is about 140.731, so the average is about 14.073 km/h.
items.skill: Compute an average value in context

items.prompt: Find the area of the region enclosed by the graphs of y = ln(x + 2) and y = x^2 − 1.
items.answer: The graphs meet at x = −1 and x ≈ 1.501; the area is about 2.926.
steps: Solve ln(x + 2) = x^2 − 1: x = −1 (check: ln 1 = 0 = 1 − 1) and x ≈ 1.501 (store it).
Between them ln(x + 2) is on top: ∫ from −1 to 1.501 of (ln(x + 2) − x^2 + 1) dx ≈ 2.926.
items.skill: Find an area with stored intersections

items.prompt: Let F(x) = ∫ from 1 to x of (3 − t·e^(0.3t)) dt for 1 ≤ x ≤ 5. Find the absolute maximum value of F on [1, 5] and where it occurs. Justify.
items.answer: The maximum is about 0.673, at x ≈ 1.766.
steps: F′(x) = 3 − x·e^(0.3x), which is 0 at x ≈ 1.766, positive before, and negative after.
Candidates: F(1) = 0, F(1.766) ≈ 0.673, F(5) ≈ −23.397, so the absolute maximum is about 0.673 at x ≈ 1.766.
items.skill: Find the extreme value of an accumulation function

items.prompt: The base of a solid is the region between the semicircle y = √(9 − x^2) and the x-axis. Cross sections perpendicular to the x-axis are equilateral triangles. Write the integral for the volume and evaluate it.
steps: An equilateral triangle with side s has area (√3/4)s^2; here s = √(9 − x^2), so the area is (√3/4)(9 − x^2).
∫ from −3 to 3 of (9 − x^2) dx = 36, so the volume is 9√3 ≈ 15.588 (the calculator agrees).
items.skill: Set up a cross-section volume with triangles

weeks.title: Beyond the exam: a modeling investigation
weeks.objective: Build, fit, and test a differential-equation model of a draining bottle from supplied data, using rates from data, separation of variables, and accumulation, and report the model's limits.

connection.before: Estimating derivatives from data (Unit 2), separable differential equations (Unit 7), and accumulation of a rate (Units 6 and 8).
connection.after: Week 36 previews ideas from further calculus as labeled enrichment and looks at next steps in mathematics.

days: Read the data and look for a pattern: average rates of change and estimated derivatives at several heights (Worksheet A, items 1–3).
Test a candidate relationship: transform the data with √h, plot it, and fit a line (Worksheet A, items 4–6).
Build the model: solve dh/dt = −k√h by separation, verify it, and find when the bottle empties (Worksheet B).
Use the model: residuals, outflow volume, and average height with a calculator (Worksheet C, items 1–5).
Write a short report: the model, the fitted constant, the evidence, one limitation, and one improvement (Worksheet C, item 6).
explanation: The exam is over, and this week uses its tools on an open question: how does water drain from a bottle? The accompanying passage, Drainage observations, supplies the bottle’s dimensions and an invented data set for this paper investigation; no equipment is needed. It accompanies every worksheet that uses the observations. Optional at home: an adult makes a small hole near the bottom of a clean plastic bottle with a pushpin; stand the bottle in a sink, fill it, and record the height above the hole every 10 seconds with a ruler and a phone timer. Keep the work area dry to avoid slips.

A modeling cycle has five steps: notice, propose, solve, test, and report. Notice: the water falls fast at first and slowly near the end, so the rate depends on the height. Propose: a physical principle called Torricelli's law (taken as given here) says the water leaves the hole at a speed proportional to √h, which leads to the differential equation dh/dt = −k√h for a constant k > 0. A competing guess, dh/dt = −ch, would make the water decrease exponentially. Data decide between them: if dh/dt = −k√h, then h′/√h should be nearly constant, and √h should be a linear function of t.

Solve: separating variables gives h^(−1/2) dh = −k dt, so 2√h = −kt + C, and with h(0) = H, √h = √H − (k/2)t, that is, h(t) = (√H − kt/2)^2 until the bottle empties at t = 2√H/k. Fit: the slope of the line through the points (t, √h) is −k/2. Test: compare the model with every data point (the differences are residuals), and check the shape: unlike an exponential, this model reaches 0 in finite time, as the data suggest. Use: the volume in the bottle is V = π(3.5)^2·h cubic centimeters, so its rate of change is dV/dt = π(3.5)^2·dh/dt. During drainage this is negative; the positive outflow rate is −dV/dt, whose integral is the volume drained.

Report the limits honestly. The formula (√H − kt/2)^2 rises again after the bottle is empty, so the model holds only for 0 ≤ t ≤ 2√H/k, with h = 0 afterward. Near the end, surface tension, the hole's shape, and measurement error matter more, and a fit that relies on one or two points is fragile. Common mistakes are choosing the exponential model because it is familiar, fitting k from a single point, extrapolating past the empty time, and mixing up centimeters (height) with cubic centimeters (volume).

figures.alt: Scatter plot of the water height h, in centimeters, against time t, in seconds, for the nine data points in the table, from (0, 16.0) to (80, 0.6). The points fall steeply at first and then more gradually.
figures.caption: Height of water above the hole

figures.alt: Empty axes for plotting: the horizontal axis is t (s) from 0 to 100, labeled every 20 with grid lines every 10, and the vertical axis is √h from 0 to 4.5, labeled every 1 with grid lines every 0.5.
figures.caption: Axes for √h against t

figures.alt: The nine points (t, √h) from the data, from (0, 4.0) to (80, 0.775), lying close to a straight line, with the line √h = 4 − 0.04t drawn from (0, 4) to (100, 0).
figures.caption: √h against t with a fitted line

examples.prompt: Use the data to estimate h′(20) and h′(60) with difference quotients centered at those times. Then compute h′/h and h′/√h at both times. Which ratio is nearly constant, and which model does that support?
examples.answer: h′(20) ≈ −0.26 cm/s and h′(60) ≈ −0.125 cm/s. The ratio h′/h changes from about −0.025 to −0.050, while h′/√h stays near −0.08 (about −0.081 and −0.079), which supports dh/dt = −k√h with k ≈ 0.08.
steps: h′/h: −0.26/10.3 ≈ −0.025 and −0.125/2.5 = −0.050, so the relative rate doubles; an exponential model would keep it constant.
h′/√h: −0.26/√10.3 ≈ −0.081 and −0.125/√2.5 ≈ −0.079, nearly equal, as the model dh/dt = −k√h requires.

examples.prompt: Solve dh/dt = −0.08√h with h(0) = 16, and find when the model says the bottle is empty.
examples.answer: h(t) = (4 − 0.04t)^2 for 0 ≤ t ≤ 100; the bottle is empty at t = 100 seconds.
steps: Separate: h^(−1/2) dh = −0.08 dt, so 2√h = −0.08t + C.
√h = 0 when t = 4/0.04 = 100 s; after that the bottle stays empty, so the formula applies only on [0, 100].

passages.title: Drainage observations
passages.text:
These observations are invented for a paper modeling investigation. A tall cylindrical bottle of radius 3.5 cm has a small hole in its side near the bottom. Time t is measured in seconds from the start of drainage, and h is the water height in centimeters above the hole. The height is recorded every 10 seconds.

| t (s) | 0 | 10 | 20 | 30 | 40 | 50 | 60 | 70 | 80 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| h (cm) | 16.0 | 13.0 | 10.3 | 7.8 | 5.8 | 4.0 | 2.5 | 1.5 | 0.6 |
passages.attribution: Original modeling data written for Liminal.

worksheets.title: Exploring the drainage data
worksheets.directions: Graphing calculator. Use the accompanying Drainage observations passage. Give units, and round computed values to three decimal places unless an item says otherwise.

items.prompt: Find the average rate of change of h on [0, 10] and on [70, 80], with units. What do the two values say about how the bottle drains?
items.answer: −0.30 cm/s on [0, 10] and −0.09 cm/s on [70, 80]: the water level falls more than three times as fast when the bottle is full as when it is nearly empty.
steps: The drop rate shrinks as the height shrinks, so the rate depends on h.
items.skill: Compute and compare average rates from data

items.prompt: Estimate h′(40) with the difference quotient centered at t = 40. Then use dh/dt = −k√h to estimate k from that value.
items.skill: Estimate a model constant from a derivative estimate

items.prompt: The ratio h′/h nearly doubles between t = 20 and t = 60, while h′/√h stays near −0.08. Which model fits the data best?
steps: A model dh/dt = −k·(something) fits when h′ divided by that something is nearly constant.
h′/√h is nearly constant, while h′ itself shrinks (ruling out a constant rate) and h′/h grows in size (ruling out exponential decay).
items.skill: Choose a model from ratio evidence

items.prompt: Compute √h for each data point and the successive differences of √h. What pattern do the differences show, and what does it say about √h as a function of t?
items.answer: √h ≈ 4.000, 3.606, 3.209, 2.793, 2.408, 2.000, 1.581, 1.225, 0.775. The differences are all close to −0.4 (from −0.356 to −0.450), so √h decreases by about 0.4 every 10 seconds: √h is nearly a linear function of t with slope about −0.04 per second.
steps: Nearly equal differences over equal time steps mean a nearly constant rate of change, which is the signature of a linear function.
items.skill: Linearize data with a transformation

items.prompt: On the axes provided, plot the points (t, √h) and draw a line that fits them. Estimate the line's slope and vertical intercept, and write its equation.
items.answer: A line through the data is close to √h = 4.0 − 0.040t (slope about −0.040 per second, intercept about 4.0).
steps: The first and last points are (0, 4.000) and (80, 0.775): slope ≈ (0.775 − 4.000)/80 ≈ −0.040.
The intercept is about 4.0, matching √16 = 4.
items.skill: Plot transformed data and fit a line

items.prompt: Use your line √h = 4.0 − 0.040t to estimate the height at t = 45 seconds and the time when the bottle is empty.
items.answer: h(45) ≈ (4.0 − 1.8)^2 = 4.84 cm; the bottle is empty when √h = 0, at t ≈ 100 seconds.
steps: √h = 0 when t = 4.0/0.040 = 100 seconds.
items.skill: Use a fitted line to make estimates

worksheets.title: Building the model by separation
worksheets.directions: No calculator. Show the separation of variables and the constant of integration. H is the starting height and k > 0 is a constant.

items.prompt: Solve dh/dt = −k√h with h(0) = H > 0 by separation of variables. Write h as a function of t, and find the time T at which h = 0.
items.answer: √h = √H − (k/2)t, so h(t) = (√H − kt/2)^2 for 0 ≤ t ≤ T, with T = 2√H/k.
steps: Separate: h^(−1/2) dh = −k dt; integrate: 2√h = −kt + C.
At t = 0, C = 2√H, so √h = √H − kt/2 and h = (√H − kt/2)^2.
h = 0 when √H = kt/2, that is, t = 2√H/k.
items.skill: Solve a separable model with symbols

items.prompt: With k = 0.08 and H = 16, find the time when the water is 4 cm above the hole and the time when the bottle is empty.
items.answer: h = 4 at t = 50 seconds; empty at t = 100 seconds.
steps: h(t) = (4 − 0.04t)^2. h = 4 means 4 − 0.04t = 2 (the nonnegative root), so t = 50.
Empty when 4 − 0.04t = 0, at t = 100 seconds.
items.skill: Use the solved model

items.prompt: Verify that h(t) = (4 − 0.04t)^2 satisfies dh/dt = −0.08√h for 0 ≤ t ≤ 100. Explain why the same formula does not describe the bottle for t > 100.
items.answer: h′(t) = 2(4 − 0.04t)(−0.04) = −0.08(4 − 0.04t) = −0.08√h, because 4 − 0.04t ≥ 0 on [0, 100]. For t > 100 the formula increases again, but an empty bottle stays empty, so h = 0 there.
steps: √h = |4 − 0.04t|, which equals 4 − 0.04t only while t ≤ 100.
For t > 100, (4 − 0.04t)^2 grows, which would mean water returning; the physical model is h = 0.
items.skill: Verify a solution and its domain

items.prompt: From dh/dt = −k√h, find d^2h/dt^2 in terms of k, and evaluate it for k = 0.08. What does the result say about the graph of h and about tangent-line estimates of the height?
items.answer: d^2h/dt^2 = k^2/2 = 0.0032, a positive constant: the graph of h is concave up, so the rate of draining slows steadily and tangent-line estimates of the height are underestimates.
steps: With k = 0.08, k^2/2 = 0.0032 cm/s^2 > 0, so h′ increases toward 0 at a constant rate.
items.skill: Derive concavity from a differential equation

items.prompt: An exponential model with the same starting height and starting rate is h(t) = 16e^(−0.02t). Compare it with the data point h(80) = 0.6 without a calculator, and explain which model is more believable near the end.
items.answer: The exponential model gives h(80) = 16e^(−1.6) > 16/9 > 1.7 cm (in fact about 3.2 cm), far above the measured 0.6 cm, and it never reaches 0; the √h model, which empties at 100 s, matches the data far better.
steps: An exponential decreases by the same factor every equal time step and never reaches 0, while the data fall to 0.6 cm and are still dropping steadily.
items.skill: Compare competing models

items.prompt: In this model k = (a/A)√(2g), where a is the area of the hole, A is the cross-sectional area of the bottle, and g is the acceleration due to gravity. How does the empty time change if the hole's area is doubled? If the bottle's radius is doubled with the same hole?
items.answer: Doubling a doubles k, which halves the empty time (to 50 s). Doubling the radius multiplies A by 4, which divides k by 4 and multiplies the empty time by 4 (to 400 s).
steps: The empty time is T = 2√H/k, inversely proportional to k.
k is proportional to a and inversely proportional to A = πr^2.
items.skill: Reason about parameters in a model

worksheets.title: Testing, using, and reporting the model
worksheets.directions: Graphing calculator. Use the accompanying Drainage observations passage and the model h(t) = (4 − 0.04t)^2 centimeters for 0 ≤ t ≤ 100 seconds. Write each setup before its value; give three decimal places.

items.prompt: Compute the residuals (data value minus model value) at each of the nine data times. What is the largest residual in absolute value, and what does it suggest?
items.answer: Residuals: 0, 0.04, 0.06, −0.04, 0.04, 0, −0.06, 0.06, −0.04 cm. The largest is 0.06 cm in absolute value, about the size of reading a ruler to the nearest millimeter, so the model fits within measurement error.
steps: Subtract from the data: 13.0 − 12.96 = 0.04, 10.3 − 10.24 = 0.06, and so on; the residuals alternate in sign with no trend.
items.skill: Test a model with residuals

items.prompt: The volume of water above the hole is V = π(3.5)^2·h cubic centimeters. Find dV/dt at t = 20 seconds, with units, and interpret it.
items.answer: dV/dt ≈ −9.852 cm^3/s: at t = 20 s water leaves the bottle at about 9.852 cubic centimeters per second.
items.skill: Convert a height rate to a volume rate

items.prompt: Use an integral of the outflow rate to find the volume of water that drains from the bottle during the first 60 seconds. Check your answer with V(0) − V(60).
steps: The outflow rate is −dV/dt = 12.25π·0.08(4 − 0.04t) cm^3/s.
Its integral over [0, 60] is about 517.232 cm^3; V(0) − V(60) = 12.25π(16 − 2.56) ≈ 517.232 cm^3 agrees.
items.skill: Accumulate an outflow rate

items.prompt: Find the average height of the water above the hole over the time the bottle drains, 0 ≤ t ≤ 100.
steps: Average value = (1/(100 − 0))∫ from 0 to 100 of h(t) dt.
The integral is about 533.333, so the average is about 5.333 cm, one third of the starting height.
items.skill: Compute the average value of a model

items.prompt: Refit k using only the first and last data points, (0, 16.0) and (80, 0.6), and the solution √h = 4 − (k/2)t. Find the new k and the new empty time. Why might a fit that uses all the points be better?
items.answer: k = 2(4 − √0.6)/80 ≈ 0.081 (more precisely 0.0806), with empty time 8/k ≈ 99.212 seconds. A fit from two points depends heavily on their measurement errors, especially the last, smallest height; using all points averages those errors out.
steps: Empty time 2√16/k = 8/k ≈ 99.212 s, close to the 100 s from the fitted line.
items.skill: Refit a parameter and judge the fit

items.prompt: Write a short report (one paragraph or a few bullet points) on the draining-bottle investigation. Include the differential equation and its solution, the fitted value of k and how you obtained it, two pieces of evidence that the model fits, one limitation, and one improvement to the data collection.

rubric.criterion: States dh/dt = −k√h and the solution h = (4 − kt/2)^2 for 0 ≤ t ≤ 8/k.
Gives k ≈ 0.08 with its method (slope of √h against t, ratio h′/√h, or a refit).
Cites the nearly constant ratio h′/√h or the linear pattern of √h against t.
Cites small residuals (at most 0.06 cm) or the finite empty time matching the data.
Names a genuine limitation, such as the model failing after the bottle empties or effects at very small heights.
Proposes a concrete improvement, such as more frequent or repeated measurements, or a finer height scale.

items.answer: Sample report: The height of water above the hole was modeled by dh/dt = −k√h, whose solution is h = (4 − kt/2)^2 until the bottle empties at t = 8/k. Plotting √h against t gave a nearly straight line with slope −0.040, so k ≈ 0.080 and the bottle empties at about 100 s. Evidence: h′/√h stays near −0.08 at different times while h′/h does not, and the residuals are at most 0.06 cm. Limitation: the formula is valid only until the bottle empties, and the last readings are most affected by measurement error. Improvement: record heights every 5 seconds and repeat the run three times to average the readings.
steps: A report answers what was modeled, how the parameter was found, why the model is believable, and where it should not be trusted.
Each claim should cite a number from the investigation.
items.skill: Report a model with evidence and limits

weeks.title: Beyond the exam: enrichment and next steps
weeks.objective: Preview three ideas from further calculus (Euler's method, integration by parts with improper integrals, and Taylor polynomials), each labeled as enrichment beyond AB, and plan next steps in mathematics.

connection.before: Slope fields and tangent lines (Units 2, 4, and 7), the Fundamental Theorem and antiderivatives (Unit 6), and week 35's modeling investigation.
connection.after: The course ends here. Next steps include further single-variable calculus, multivariable calculus, linear algebra, statistics, and calculus-based physics.

days: Enrichment, not AB content: Euler's method as repeated tangent-line steps along a slope field (Worksheet A).
Enrichment, not AB content: integration by parts, the product rule read backward (Worksheet B, items 1–3).
Enrichment, not AB content: improper integrals as limits of definite integrals (Worksheet B, items 4–6).
Enrichment, not AB content: Taylor polynomials, which extend the tangent line to higher degree (Worksheet C).
Next steps: compare course options with their actual prerequisites, and keep a list of the calculus ideas you want to study further.
explanation: Everything this week is enrichment: none of it is AB content, and none of it appears on the AP® Calculus AB Exam. Each idea grows out of something the course already built. Euler's method extends tangent-line approximation: to follow the solution of dy/dx = F(x, y) from a starting point, take a small step h along the tangent line, recompute the slope at the new point, and repeat: x(n+1) = x(n) + h and y(n+1) = y(n) + h·F(x(n), y(n)). Smaller steps track the curve more closely; when the solution is concave up, tangent steps fall below it, so Euler values are underestimates.

Integration by parts reverses the product rule. Since (uv)′ = u′v + uv′, integrating gives ∫ u dv = uv − ∫ v du. Choose u so that it becomes simpler when differentiated (a polynomial, or ln x) and dv so that it is easy to integrate. For example, ∫ x·e^x dx = x·e^x − ∫ e^x dx = (x − 1)e^x + C. An improper integral has an infinite limit of integration and is defined as a limit: ∫ from 1 to ∞ of f(x) dx = lim as b→∞ of ∫ from 1 to b of f(x) dx. When the limit is a finite number the integral converges, so an unbounded region can have a finite area; otherwise it diverges.

A Taylor polynomial matches a function's value and several derivatives at one point. The tangent line matches the value and the first derivative; the degree-n Taylor polynomial at x = a, P(x) = f(a) + f′(a)(x − a) + f″(a)(x − a)^2/2! + … + f^(n)(a)(x − a)^n/n!, matches the first n derivatives as well. Near a, higher degree usually means a better approximation: for e^x at 0, P(x) = 1 + x + x^2/2 + x^3/6 approximates e^0.1 to within about 0.000004.

Next steps depend on interests and on the receiving course's actual prerequisites, so check them directly. Further single-variable calculus continues with these ideas and with infinite series; multivariable calculus extends derivatives and integrals to functions of several variables; linear algebra and differential equations are the language of much of science and engineering; statistics and calculus-based physics use integrals and rates constantly. Keep your notes and error log: the habits that earned free-response points (naming the function, stating hypotheses, writing the setup) carry into every one of these courses.

figures.alt: The curve y = 2e^x − x − 1 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1, rising from (0, 1) to about (1, 3.44), with two straight Euler steps of width 0.5 drawn below it: from (0, 1) to (0.5, 1.5) and from (0.5, 1.5) to (1, 2.5).
figures.caption: Euler's method falls below a concave-up solution

examples.prompt: Enrichment (not AB content). Use Euler's method with step size h = 0.5 to approximate y(1) for the solution of dy/dx = x + y with y(0) = 1. The exact solution is y = 2e^x − x − 1; compare.
examples.answer: Euler gives y(1) ≈ 2.5, while the exact value is 2e − 2 ≈ 3.437; the Euler value is an underestimate.
steps: The solution is concave up (y″ = 1 + y′ > 0 here), so each tangent step falls below the curve; 2e − 2 ≈ 3.437.

examples.prompt: Enrichment (not AB content). Evaluate ∫ from 0 to ∞ of x·e^(−x) dx.
examples.answer: The integral converges to 1.
steps: By parts with u = x and dv = e^(−x) dx: ∫ x·e^(−x) dx = −x·e^(−x) − e^(−x) + C = −(x + 1)e^(−x) + C.
∫ from 0 to b of x·e^(−x) dx = 1 − (b + 1)e^(−b).
As b→∞, (b + 1)e^(−b) → 0 (L'Hospital's Rule on (b + 1)/e^b), so the integral is 1.

worksheets.title: Enrichment: Euler's method (not AB content)
worksheets.directions: Graphing calculator. Enrichment beyond AB. Show each Euler step as a row: x, y, slope, and the next y. Give decimal answers to three places where they do not terminate sooner.

items.prompt: Use Euler's method with h = 0.5 and two steps to approximate y(1) for dy/dx = 2x − y with y(0) = 1.
items.skill: Carry out two Euler steps

items.prompt: Repeat item 1 with h = 0.25 and four steps. The exact solution is y = 2x − 2 + 3e^(−x). Compare both Euler values with the exact value of y(1).
items.answer: With h = 0.25, y(1) ≈ 0.949; the exact value is 3/e ≈ 1.104. The errors are about 0.354 (h = 0.5) and 0.154 (h = 0.25).
items.skill: Compare Euler approximations with an exact solution

items.prompt: With h = 0.125 (eight steps), Euler's method gives y(1) ≈ 1.031 for the equation in item 1. Use the three errors to describe how the error changes when the step size is halved.
items.answer: The errors are about 0.354, 0.154, and 0.073: halving h roughly halves the error.
steps: The ratios 0.154/0.354 ≈ 0.43 and 0.073/0.154 ≈ 0.47 approach 1/2, so the error is roughly proportional to h.
items.skill: Describe how step size affects Euler error

items.prompt: The solution of a differential equation is concave up on [0, 1]. Euler's method with a positive step is used to approximate y(1) starting from x = 0. Which statement is true?
choices: Concavity tells nothing about the approximation.
steps: Each Euler step follows a tangent line, and tangent lines lie below a concave-up curve.
So the Euler values fall below the solution: underestimates.
items.skill: Connect concavity to Euler's method

items.prompt: A population satisfies dy/dt = 0.3y with y(0) = 100, where t is in years. Use Euler's method with h = 1 to approximate y(3), and compare with the exact value 100e^(0.9).
items.answer: Euler gives 100(1.3)^3 = 219.7; the exact value is 100e^(0.9) ≈ 245.960, so Euler underestimates by about 26.
steps: Each step multiplies y by 1 + 0.3 = 1.3: 130, 169, 219.7.
e^(0.9) ≈ 2.4596, so the exact value is about 245.960.
items.skill: Apply Euler's method to growth

items.prompt: Use Euler's method with h = 0.1 and ten steps for dy/dx = y·cos x with y(0) = 1 to approximate y(1). The exact solution is y = e^(sin x); compare.
items.answer: Euler gives y(1) ≈ 2.288; the exact value e^(sin 1) ≈ 2.320.
steps: Iterate y(new) = y + 0.1·y·cos x with x = 0, 0.1, …, 0.9 (a calculator list or program helps).
The result is about 2.288, about 0.032 below e^(sin 1) ≈ 2.320.
items.skill: Iterate Euler's method with a calculator

worksheets.title: Enrichment: integration by parts and improper integrals (not AB content)
worksheets.directions: No calculator. Enrichment beyond AB. For integration by parts, name u and dv. For improper integrals, write the limit before evaluating it.

items.prompt: Find ∫ x·cos x dx.
steps: u = x, dv = cos x dx, so du = dx and v = sin x.
∫ x·cos x dx = x·sin x − ∫ sin x dx = x·sin x + cos x + C.
items.skill: Integrate by parts once

items.prompt: Evaluate ∫ from 1 to e of ln x dx.
steps: u = ln x, dv = dx, so du = dx/x and v = x: ∫ ln x dx = x·ln x − x + C.
[x·ln x − x] from 1 to e = (e − e) − (0 − 1) = 1.
items.skill: Integrate a logarithm by parts

items.prompt: Find ∫ x·e^(2x) dx.
steps: u = x, dv = e^(2x) dx, so v = e^(2x)/2.
items.skill: Integrate a polynomial times an exponential

items.prompt: Evaluate ∫ from 1 to ∞ of 1/x^2 dx.
steps: ∫ from 1 to b of x^(−2) dx = 1 − 1/b.
lim as b→∞ of (1 − 1/b) = 1, so the integral converges to 1.
items.skill: Evaluate a convergent improper integral

items.prompt: Which improper integral converges?
steps: The others grow without bound: 2√b − 2, ln b, and 2e^(b/2) − 2e^(1/2).
items.skill: Decide convergence

items.prompt: Evaluate ∫ from 0 to ∞ of e^(−3x) dx, and describe the region whose area it gives.
items.answer: 1/3; it is the area of the unbounded region under y = e^(−3x) and above the x-axis for x ≥ 0, which is finite.
steps: ∫ from 0 to b of e^(−3x) dx = (1 − e^(−3b))/3.
As b→∞, e^(−3b) → 0, so the limit is 1/3.
items.skill: Interpret a convergent improper integral as area

worksheets.title: Enrichment: polynomial approximations (not AB content)
worksheets.directions: Graphing calculator. Enrichment beyond AB. Build each Taylor polynomial from derivative values, and use the calculator to compare with the function's value.

items.prompt: Find the degree-2 Taylor polynomial of f(x) = √x at x = 4, and use it to approximate √4.2. Compare with the calculator's value.
steps: f(4) = 2, f′(x) = 1/(2√x) gives 1/4, and f″(x) = −1/(4x^(3/2)) gives −1/32, so the quadratic coefficient is −1/64.
items.skill: Build a degree-2 Taylor polynomial

items.prompt: Use the degree-3 Taylor polynomial of e^x at x = 0 to approximate e^0.1, and compare with the calculator's value.
steps: Every derivative of e^x is e^x, which is 1 at x = 0, so P(x) = 1 + x + x^2/2 + x^3/6.
items.skill: Approximate an exponential with a polynomial

items.prompt: Use the degree-4 Taylor polynomial of cos x at x = 0 to approximate cos(0.5), and compare with the calculator's value.
steps: The derivatives of cos x at 0 cycle 1, 0, −1, 0, 1.
items.skill: Approximate a cosine with a polynomial

items.prompt: A function f has f(2) = 3, f′(2) = −1, f″(2) = 4, and f‴(2) = 6. Write the degree-3 Taylor polynomial of f at x = 2, and use it to approximate f(2.1).
steps: Coefficients: f″(2)/2! = 2 and f‴(2)/3! = 1.
items.skill: Build a Taylor polynomial from derivative values

items.prompt: For ln(1 + x) at x = 0, compare the tangent line L(x) = x and the degree-2 Taylor polynomial P(x) = x − x^2/2 as approximations of ln(1.2).
items.answer: L(0.2) = 0.2 and P(0.2) = 0.18, while ln(1.2) ≈ 0.182; the errors are about 0.018 and 0.002, so the quadratic is about eight times closer.
items.skill: Compare approximations of increasing degree

items.prompt: Which polynomial is the degree-2 Taylor polynomial of e^(2x) at x = 0?
items.skill: Identify a Taylor polynomial
